variants.reconstruction:
%n šarru? ea ina mayyāli ina šadādi
#note: Judging from the photograph of the tablet in @bib{RN493@174=Pl. 1}, there does not seem to be room for another sign to the left of @akk{RU} at the beginning of the line. For the various suggestions made for this line, which all but one involve restoring such an extra sign, see @bib{RN303@129}, as well as @bib{RN493@9; 13f.}, who is the only one to read the line with @akk{RU} only, namely as @i{nadi} “(he was) lying”. For the latter see, however, @bib{RN1364@395}, who points out that such logographic writings are quite uncommon in literary compositions. For the emendation to @i{šarru} “king” employed here, see l. c+8 @i{ana šarri ea}. In essence, it goes back to a suggestion by M. Gallery @i{apud} @bib{RN162@345 fn. 5}.

variants.intertext: The restoration of the lines in section d+N follows @bib{Schramm.OrNS43@163-164}. It either comprises the dialogue between Adapa and the two gods Tammuz and Gizzida, or Ea’s prediction thereof. In the former case, d+1 would be the same line as c+14. In the latter case, the end of Ea’s instructions, the arrival of Anu’s messenger and Adapa’s journey to heaven would be missing between the sections c+N and d+N.

variants.intertext: Depending on the placement of section d+N (see above), possibly the arrival of Anu’s messenger and Adapa’s journey to heaven should first follow here. In any case, what would follow next would be Adapa being brought before Anu, who would then question him about his reasons for breaking the wings of the south wind. After that, Tammuz and Gizzida would calm the king of the gods, who would then agree to serve Adapa the goods that Ea had predicted. This is where section e+N begins.
